extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for novel-writing covering character (flat vs round), point of view, and plot — aimed at assessing or producing sustained fiction. Emphasizes how devices function, reader effects, and examples from canonical writers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flat vs round characters (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Flat characters are constructed round a single idea or quality and can be expressed in one sentence; round characters cannot be summed up simply and have complexity, private desires, and capacity for change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and formulations: Flat: 'I never will desert Mr. Micawber.' Caleb Balderstone—the idea is the man. Proust’s Princess of Parma: 'I must be particularly careful to be kind.' Round: Becky Sharp, most principal characters in War and Peace, Dostoevsky characters, Madame Bovary. Test of roundness: 'capable of surprising in a convincing way.' If it never surprises, it is flat; if it surprises but does not convince, it is 'a flat pretending to be round.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantages and uses of flat characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Flat characters are useful devices because they are immediately recognizable, need no reintroduction, and provide a ready-made atmosphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorial convenience: 'they never need reintroducing, never run away, have not to be watched for development, and provide their own atmosphere.' Reader convenience: 'easily remembered by the reader afterwards' and give books a feeling of permanence. Good for comedy and for creating memorable types; used effectively by Dickens and some works of Wells. Useful in combination with round characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits and anti-patterns of flat characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Flat characters are less suited to serious or tragic treatment and can bore readers when used for sustained tragic or serious drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning: 'A serious or tragic flat character is apt to be a bore.' Example: a farmer whose single formula ('I'll plough up that bit of gorse') becomes tedious rather than interesting. Remedy: analyze and connect the formula to other aspects of the person so it becomes an obsession in a man—turning flat into round.

rubrics_metrics.name: Round characters (capacity and test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Round characters are those capable of surprising convincingly, having incalculability and life within the pages; they possess inner private life and can be modified by events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: principal characters in War and Peace, Dostoevsky characters, Madame Bovary, Becky Sharp. The test: 'The test of a round character is whether it is capable of surprising in a convincing way.' If it never surprises, it is flat; if it surprises but does not convince, it is flat pretending to be round.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial technique: modulating flat into round
rubrics_metrics.description: A novelist should be able to momentarily expand a flat character into roundness when circumstances demand, then allow retreat to the formulaic impression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Jane Austen’s Lady Bertram is mostly flat ('I am kindly, but must not be fatigued') but can be inflated into roundness in a single sentence when catastrophe requires it; the character then 'collapses back into a flat one' when ordinary life resumes. This modulation increases plausibility and the probability of plot events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of view (catalogue of options)
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrator’s relation to the story may be outside (impartial/partial onlooker), omniscient, inhabiting a character (dramatic/first-person), or intermediate attitudes; choice of POV is a fundamental device.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Percy Lubbock's taxonomy referenced. Examples: Dickens shifts between omniscience, partial omniscience, and dramatic first-person (Esther Summerson) in Bleak House. Gide and Tolstoy also shift POV. The novelist may use intermittent knowledge; the key is whether shifts are convincing and whether the writer can 'bounce' the reader into acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shifting point of view and 'bouncing' the reader
rubrics_metrics.description: Shifting the narrator’s perspective can work provided the writer has the power to make the reader accept those shifts—'to bounce the reader into accepting what he says.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of success: Dickens (Bleak House) and Tolstoy (War and Peace) shift POV and are accepted by readers; Gide shows his jolts too much and is less effective. Critic's objections often overstate the importance of fixed POV; what matters is convincingness and the writer’s skill in handling transitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial intrusion about individual characters (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Taking the reader into the author’s confidence about individual characters (direct authorial asides about characters) is dangerous and harmful to illusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted anti-pattern: 'Doesn't A look nice—she always was my favourite' leads to 'bar-parlour chattiness' and causes a drop in temperature and emotional laxity. Drawing back to generalize about life/universe is acceptable (Hardy, Conrad), but confidences about individual people 'beckon the reader away from the people to an examination of the novelist’s mind.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Novel's privilege: access to secret life and subconscious
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelist uniquely commands the 'secret life' and the subconscious, showing internal monologue and inner causes of action which the drama cannot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The novelist may show subconscious short-circuiting into action or the private soliloquy; shifts between limited and omniscient knowledge may invite questions but what matters is whether the presentation of the secret life is convincing ('All that matters to the reader is whether the shifting of attitude and the secret life are convincing').

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot vs story (definition and distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: A story is a narrative of events in time-sequence; a plot is a narrative emphasizing causality ('The king died, and then the queen died of grief' is a plot). Plot asks 'why?' rather than merely 'and then?'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot demands intelligence and memory of the reader, suspends time-sequence (mystery pockets) and is capable of high development. Plots cannot be consumed merely for curiosity; they require the reader to hold facts and reason back and forth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader faculties required for plot: intelligence and memory
rubrics_metrics.description: To appreciate a plot, the reader must exercise intelligence (relating facts across the work) and memory (retaining earlier facts so causality makes sense).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intelligence: picking up facts and seeing them in relation to previous pages; memory: essential so that causes and effects are traceable. Without these faculties the plot reduces to mere story-level 'and then—and then' curiosity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mystery as essential element in plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Mystery (suspension of full explanation) is essential to plot; it creates 'pockets in time' and provokes brooding rather than mere curiosity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forms: explicit mysteries ('Why did the queen die?') and subtle half-explained gestures whose meanings dawn later. To appreciate mystery the reader must leave part of the mind brooding while continuing to read.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy and organic unity in plot
rubrics_metrics.description: In a good plot every action or word ought to count; the plot should be economical, spare, organic, and free from dead matter or loose ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid misleading the reader; the plot-maker expects no loose ends. Even when complicated, the plot should rearrange facts into an esthetically compact whole rather than a jumble of clues. 'Every action or word in a plot ought to count ; it ought to be economical and spare; even when complicated it should be organic and free from dead matter.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprise and shock as indicators of a successful plot
rubrics_metrics.description: A plot ought to cause surprise—an incident that shocks and then resolves into the sense of 'Oh, that's all right' indicates a healthy plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Meredith's contrivances (the horse-whipping of Dr. Shrapnel) give shock that transforms characters and reacts upon the world of the book. Surprise should arise plausibly from character and situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrivance: permitted if springing from character
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrivances or artful devices in plot are acceptable when they 'spring from the characters and react upon them' rather than being arbitrary mechanisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meredith's plots described as 'a series of contrivances' that are 'often delightful, sometimes touching, always unexpected' because they arise from character. Bad contrivance would be arbitrary action that characters would not naturally produce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters' relation to plot in the novel (tension with dramatic requirements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlike drama where characters are cut to plot's requirements, in the novel characters are large and intractable; plot must persuade them to contribute without stripping their private life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters 'must not brood too long' if the plot requires action, but forcing characters into plot behavior can be unsatisfactory; a balance is needed so incidents spring from character rather than override it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to intermittent/partial knowledge (novelistic advantage)
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelist may legitimately expand and contract perception—sometimes omniscient, sometimes limited—mirroring human intermittence of understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This intermittent knowledge enriches variety and color in the novel and has a parallel in real life ('We are stupider at some times than others'); acceptable when handled by a skilled writer (Dickens, Tolstoy).
